s03.slug: MONDAY · 1:02 PM · HOLLIS HALL, 302 — THE CONVERSION OF ST. PAUL
body: He takes the Hollis stairs two at a time and comes into 302 at two minutes past one, still ahead of Hale, with his pulse somewhere back down Del Playa and his face warm to the ears. He sits at the door end under the clock and puts both hands around a pen, because they want something to hold.

It’s Monday’s room. Evan is at the door with the roster on its clipboard, ticking names with a click of the pen. Yusuf has the corner and a coffee. The two girls from the window side are comparing their *Frankenstein*s, whose spines broke at the same chapter. At the window end, in the last chair, Lena has *The End of the Affair* out already for Thursday, set true to the edge of the table, with her *Frankenstein* under it, finished, and the pencil laid across the pair.

Caleb has his phone under the lip of the table again, tilted toward Yusuf, and says it at the volume of a man who believes he is whispering. “Costigan’s on a celebrity blog. Not Perez. One of the ones that wants to be Perez.”
Yusuf looks at the phone, and at Jack. “Congratulations?”
At the window end, Lena turns a page.

Hale comes in at six minutes past with wine on his cuff and his coat over his arm, takes the roster from Evan without reading it, and sees the phone. He sits down halfway along the side, where he has to turn his head for either end, and looks delighted with the calendar.

“Today,” he tells the table, “is the Conversion of St. Paul. I looked it up, so that you wouldn’t have to. It is the only conversion story I have ever found credible. A man falls off a horse and is never the same again.” He lifts a finger. “There is no horse in Acts, incidentally. Caravaggio supplied the horse. The Church has always been generous with livestock.”
He turns his head down the table to Caleb, unhurried, and says it the way it ought to be said, each word set down where it goes:
“*Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?*”
“Dude,” says Caleb, and the phone goes into his bag.

They finish *Frankenstein*. Hale does the ending himself, because none of them, he says, can be trusted with it. “Victor dies apologizing to a sea captain, which is the most English thing a Swiss has ever done. The creature gets the last speech, and the best one, and then Mrs. Shelley puts him on a raft of ice and sends him off to burn himself somewhere none of us can check. *Lost in darkness and distance.* She was nineteen, and she knew where to stop.” He looks around the table. “Several of you are nineteen.”
“He said he’d do it,” Yusuf says. “He kept every other promise in the book.”
“Noorzai has read the book,” says Hale. “Make a note, Mr. Marsh. It may not happen again.”

With ten minutes left he folds his hands on the roster. “Thursday I shall be in New York, being rude to a churchman on a stage, for money. Greene therefore moves. Wednesday, six o’clock, at my house. Some of you know the way.” At the window end the pencil stops. “The President is addressing the nation at the same hour. I intend to have him on, and we shall treat him as the warm-up act. Bring a guest. The speech is long and the wine is cheap.” Evan writes it on the clipboard. “Phones go in the dog’s bowl at the door. House rule. Berkeley is deaf, and I should like the rest of you to try it.”

He turns his head to the door end, and then the long way round to the window end, so the table can watch him do it. “Mr. Costigan will defend Sarah Miles’s silence. Miss Broussard will prosecute it. You both spent last week arguing against yourselves on paper. I should like you back in your own clothes.”
Jack keeps his eyes on Hale.

“Fine,” Lena says — to Hale. She takes the pencil off the Greene and writes something small in the top margin of the first page, the address, probably, though she has been to that house before; and she lays the pencil back across the book where it was.

s12.slug: WEDNESDAY · 5:50 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, THE CLIFF END — HALE’S
body: The rain stopped on Monday and the cliff end of Del Playa still hasn’t been told. Sandbags slump along the curb in front of the last three houses, gone dark with what’s in them, and the wooden stairs down to the beach are brown with mud to the third step. At the end of the lane the sky over the water is going from orange to a hard, clean blue; behind him, over the mountains, the moon is already up and nearly round.
At Hale’s gate he opens the RAZR one more time before it has to go in the bowl.

body: He shuts it. Inside the screen door, on the mat, there’s a steel dog bowl with BERKELEY painted on the side in a careful hand, and it’s already a bowl full of phones. He lays his on top, on a pink BlackBerry he knows. Hale meets him inside the door in his shirtsleeves with a corkscrew. “Mr. Costigan. You’ve brought nothing,” he says. “I admire that in a guest. It’s so rare.”

Hale’s house is the one he remembers from the fall: books to the ceiling on every wall that isn’t window, the woodstove going in the corner, and the table, the six-panel door on its trestles, under a white cloth tonight with a loaf on a board, a wedge of something orange and a row of glasses that don’t match. Berkeley is asleep on his side on the Turkish rug. A small television sits on a stack of encyclopedias at the far end of the room, tuned to the Capitol with the sound down, where men in dark suits are filing in under a flag the size of a house. Evan is going round with a bottle. Caleb has a chair already; Yusuf has brought his coffee from the Commons in a paper cup, with the lid on.

Lena is already here. She’s at the bookshelves with Laney, who is her guest, and her copy of the Greene is on the cloth at a place in the middle of the door, with a full glass of Hale’s red beside it and a second chair pulled in close. She has her hair up with a pencil through the knot and the medal outside her sweater tonight, and he knows where she is in the room every minute without having to look.

body.text: When he comes in, her eyes go to the door and away. The curb heard him on Saturday, and by now half of Newman has heard about it.
When he comes in she doesn’t look up from the shelf.

body: Theo comes up the walk at five to six in the pressed blazer with the bottle held out before him in both hands, and gives Hale the story on the step. It’s Monday’s story, and it has grown. The ambassador now has a name and a widowed sister in San Marino, and he wept, specifically, during the fish; the crate was stenciled in Logroño; the cellar in Pasadena is kept at fifty-five degrees by a man called Ignacio, who has been with the family thirty years and will not be rushed. Hale listens to all of it with his head on one side, turning the bottle in his hands.
“Mr. Vance,” he says. “There’s a price on it.”
“He was a humble man,” says Theo.
Hale gives it to Evan. “Open it. We’ll find out what humility tastes like.”

Laney has brought a Texas sheet cake in a Pyrex dish with the foil crimped down at the corners, still warm, because in Dallas, she informs Hale, you do not show up to a speech without a sheet cake. “Then the speech has already been improved,” Hale says, and takes the foil off himself. When Jack passes her at the shelves, Laney gives him a nod that would do for a stranger at a bus stop, and nothing else.

Somebody has been at the table before him. The sheet cake ends up in front of the place with Lena’s book, and Theo, coming past, takes the open Rioja back from Evan, sets it down in front of the chair pulled in beside it, and steers Jack toward that chair with a hand in the small of his back, talking about sediment.

Hale comes out of the kitchen with a stack of jam jars for the overflow and stops. He sets the jars down. He picks up Lena’s chair, carries it the length of the room to the far end of the door, and puts it down there; then he goes back for her book and her glass, and puts those down with it. “Opposite ends,” he says, to the room in general, “for the safety of the others.”

Lena sits down where he has put her without a word about it. Laney carries the sheet cake down after her. Jack takes the near end, by the screen door, and Theo takes the chair beside him with the expression of a director whose set has been struck by the landlord.
The President comes down the aisle at six through a crowd of people who want his hand, and Hale turns the sound up. “Ladies and gentlemen,” he says. “The warm-up act.”

It’s jobs first. “Sensible,” says Hale. “No politician ever lost a room by coming out against unemployment.” Next a freeze on spending, three years of it, everything but security. “A freeze,” Hale says. “In January. He’s been reading Dante.” Caleb laughs, late, and too loud for the size of the room.
At the far end Lena laughs too, before she can stop it, and puts the back of her hand to her mouth. He has to look at the television.

When the President gets to health care — Massachusetts, and not walking away from it now — Jack writes *Stupak?* in the margin of the Greene. At the far end of the door, without looking up, Lena’s pencil is moving on hers. He’d put money on the word. They’re agreeing about it at opposite ends of a door.

Every few paragraphs the chamber splits, half of it up on its feet and half sitting on its hands, and Hale points his glass at the half that’s sitting. “Say what you like about them. They are the only people in that room doing what they actually think.” Then at the half that’s standing: “And those are the only people in it who will get anything done. That is democracy, and you are welcome to it.”

Then the President turns at the podium and speaks to the Court. The justices are down in front in their black robes, and he tells them, more or less to their faces, that last week’s decision has thrown the doors open to special interests, foreign money among them, and the room comes up on its feet around them. The camera finds one justice sitting still in the middle of it, and his head goes side to side, and his mouth makes two words: *not true*.
“Oh, *dear*,” says Hale, enchanted. “A justice with an opinion. In public. In England we’d have him stuffed.”
Jack thinks of a black umbrella turned inside out on the Lagoon bridge, and somebody under it doing two justices at once with nothing but her chin.

When the speech comes round to Afghanistan — the troops, and when they’ll start to come home — Yusuf’s coffee is on its way down to the table, and it stops halfway and doesn’t go the rest of the way. Hale keeps his mouth shut through all of it.

Laney has been cold to him all evening, which for Laney takes work. At the half hour she goes up the side of the door with a knife, cutting the sheet cake and leaving a slab of it on a napkin in front of everyone but him; and when Jack asks the table for the bread, the basket is at her elbow. She picks it up and holds it out to him with a little church-supper nod of encouragement, and her face catches up with her hand halfway across. She lets go of it so fast he nearly drops it.

Hale turns the television off at ten past seven, as the man from Virginia comes up in the corner of the screen. “Before the rebuttal,” he says, “which I refuse to dignify. He’ll be very reasonable, and I haven’t the stomach.” He pours for every glass that’s held out to him, and two that aren’t, and sits back down midway along the door, and lays the novel on the cloth in front of him.

s13.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:12 PM · HALE’S, THE DOOR ON TRESTLES
body: “Nineteen forty-four,” says Hale. “A flying bomb comes down by the Common. Bendrix goes downstairs when it lands, and the front door comes off its hinges and down on top of him, and he’s out cold under it.” He knocks twice on the panels in front of him. “You’ll forgive the furniture. Nobody has died under this one yet.”

“Sarah sees him under it and thinks he’s dead. So she kneels on the floor and makes a promise to a God she doesn’t believe in: let him be alive, and she’ll give him up. And in he walks, with plaster in his hair.” Hale opens his hands. “She keeps it. She ends the affair without one word of why, and he finds out two years later from her diary, which a private detective steals for him. Greene’s little joke, of course, is that her mother had her baptized when she was small and never told her. The paperwork was in order all along.” He turns his head to the far end. “Was she right to keep quiet? Miss Broussard.”
Lena doesn’t open the book. She has his sentence by heart, and she says it down the length of the door, word for word:

“*A man who keeps quiet to save himself has already confessed; he’s only chosen the wrong confessor.*” Then: “You wrote that, Costigan. Sarah kept quiet to save herself — from having to hear him. She owed him one sentence. *I made a promise and I’m keeping it.* That’s all it would have cost her. Instead she let him walk around London for two years thinking he’d been thrown over, because one sentence would have meant an argument, and she didn’t trust herself to win it.” Her hand is on the cover of the Greene. “Aquinas puts truthfulness under justice. Second part of the second part, question one-oh-nine. It isn’t manners. It’s owed. The truth about a man’s life belongs to the man. You don’t get to keep it for him because it’s heavy.”
It’s good. It’s better than his was, and it’s his.
“She didn’t owe Bendrix the reason,” Jack says. “She made the promise to God. Not to him. What she owed, she owed to God, and she paid it.”
“God doesn’t need her to lie to a man to keep a promise.”

“She didn’t lie. She kept quiet.” He has the Penguin shut under his hand. “Next question over. One-ten. Your man says it’s lawful to hide the truth prudently, and he got that from Augustine. That’s two Doctors of the Church on my side of the door.”
“*Prudently*,” Lena says. “For an afternoon. Not for two years while he goes out of his mind.”
Yusuf has his coffee in both hands. “Where I grew up,” he says, quietly, “a promise to God was nobody else’s business. You didn’t explain it. You kept it.”
“It’s somebody else’s business,” Lena says, not unkindly, “when it’s his life you promised away.”
Hale turns his head back to the near end, and the room turns with him.

choices.text: “A vow you explain is a vow you’ve put up for negotiation. He’d have talked her out of it. He’s a novelist. He’d have won.”
response: “So she lied to him,” Lena says, “to keep from losing an argument.” She lets the table hear how that sounds. “That’s not a vow. That’s a debate strategy. If he could have talked her out of it, it wasn’t much of a promise. And if it was, he couldn’t have. Either way she owed him the chance to try.”
He has an answer for that. It isn’t as good as hers, and he doesn’t use it.
“*There is a silence that isn’t cowardice: when the truth would only be one more thing taken from people who have already lost everything.*” He doesn’t need the page either. “You wrote that.”
Halfway down the door Caleb says “Oh,” out loud, and puts his hand over his mouth.
“Bendrix hadn’t lost everything,” Lena says. “He’d lost *her*.” She stops. When she goes on, it’s lower. “It’s not the same.”

choices.text: “She owed him a sentence. You’re right.”
response: It throws her. She looks at him down the length of the door like a player whose opponent has moved a piece she didn’t see.
“Then what are you defending?”
He doesn’t know yet. He’s going to have to find out with Hale’s table listening.

choices.text: “She did tell him. She left. It was the only sentence he’d believe.”
response: “Leaving isn’t a sentence,” Lena says. “It’s a door.” Her hand comes down flat on the six panels of one.
If it’s a joke, she doesn’t give anybody time to laugh at it.

s13a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:20 PM · HALE’S, THE DOOR ON TRESTLES
body: “At least Sarah kept a diary,” Lena says. “In a drawer. In her own house. Parkis had to steal it to read it.” She stops there, long enough for the table to think she’s finished.
“Some people publish.”
It takes the room a moment to understand that she has left the book.
“Miss Broussard,” Hale says, mildly. “The text.”

“I’m on the text.” She doesn’t look at him. “Sarah wrote to God where nobody would ever see it. That’s what the diary *is*. The most private thing in the novel, and it took a thief to get it out of the drawer.”
“A website on Monday,” she says. “A bed on Tuesday. An iPad before lunch today.”
“Picture it,” Theo says brightly, to the table at large. “A sorbet. Between courses. Something with lemon in it, to —”
“Mr. Vance is a guest,” says Hale, “and guests are furniture.”
Theo becomes furniture. Lena looks down the door at Jack. “Your friend from school.”
“You don’t know her.”
“No,” Lena says. “I’ve been kept informed.”
So it reached her. All of it, a day at a time, out at the far end of campus, by whatever road these things take.

“It was a true picture,” he says. “She didn’t do it to anybody. She did it because she’s sick to death of being told what she’s allowed to have. And she took it down herself, yesterday, on the side of the freeway, the second she saw it cost somebody something. She did that on her own. She gave to Haiti before anybody called her and asked. She reads Chesterton on the beach and argues with him in the margins, and half the time she wins. She makes me say what I think, and then she argues with that. I have never once seen her pretend with me.”
Lena doesn’t interrupt him. She lets him get all the way to the end, and then she picks the pencil up off the Greene.
“I didn’t say she wasn’t real, Jack,” she says. “I said she publishes.” She turns the pencil end over end and lays it down. “The real ones you keep in a drawer.”

choices.text: “Greene published. Sarah’s diary *is* the book. You’re prosecuting the novel.”
response: Hale is half out of his chair with pleasure. Lena doesn’t look at him.
“Greene was a married man writing about his mistress, Costigan,” she says, flat. “He’d know about publishing.”
It goes in under something, and she doesn’t wait to see where.

choices.text: “And some people date a man who agrees with everything they say.”
response: It wins the point. He hears it win.
Beside him Theo sets his glass down. At the far end Lena takes the full glass she hasn’t touched and pushes it away from her across the cloth, slowly, until it’s out of her reach.
On Sunday night he told Theo to stop kicking that man. He has just put the boot in himself, in front of a table, and it doesn’t feel like anything he wanted.

choices.text: “Fine. Sarah’s diary was in a drawer.”
response: She doesn’t take it.
“Don’t do that,” she says, quietly. “Don’t give me the drawer.”

choices.text: *Don’t take the bait. Back to Greene.*
response: He goes back to the book instead, to the end of it, where his side lives.
She lets him go. She folds her arms on the Greene and waits for him there.

s13b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:28 PM · HALE’S, THE DOOR ON TRESTLES

body.text: She doesn’t answer the shot. She hasn’t looked at him since it landed; she is looking at the novel.
“Go on, then,” she says. “Defend the ending.”

body: He goes to the ending.

“Sarah dies,” he says. “That’s the part people forget, because by then the book’s about something else. She dies, and what Greene leaves you is the two men. Bendrix and Henry — the lover and the husband. Two men who lost the same woman, living in the same house, walking across the Common to the pub together at night.” He has the Penguin open to the last pages, though he doesn’t need it. “That’s the end. They end up friends. Good friends. Bendrix hates God on the last page and can’t stop talking to him, and he has Henry. That’s what grace looks like in Greene. It’s what’s left when you can’t have the other thing. You get to be friends.”
At *friends* she looks up. At *good friends* her chair goes back, and she’s on her feet, and her hand comes down on the door.
“If we’re such *good friends*,” she says, “how come I had to find out about your girlfriend from a Facebook status, when we talked every single day for weeks leading up to it?”
It isn’t a big room, and she fills it.

Theo’s hand stops on the neck of the bottle. Beside her, Laney has the cake knife still in her fingers and her face wide open. Caleb doesn’t move. Hale doesn’t move. On the Turkish rug Berkeley, who can’t hear a thing, lifts his long gray head off his paws: the door jumped.
*Every single day.* He’d have said most nights, if anybody had asked him. She has it as every day.

Jack looks down the length of the door at her, and there is nothing in his mouth. He goes through himself for an answer fast, like a man going through his pockets for a key, and comes up with nothing he can say at this table.

choices.text: “You should have heard it from me.”
choices.key: At Hale’s, Lena asked why she had to find out about your girlfriend from a Facebook status. You told her she should have heard it from you. It wasn’t an answer.
response: “Yes,” she says. “I should have.”
Her hand is still on the door. She waits, down at the far end of it, with Hale’s table waiting along with her, and nothing else comes. At last she takes the hand back.

choices.key: At Hale’s, Lena asked why she had to find out about your girlfriend from a Facebook status. You said nothing.
response: He says nothing. She gives him all the silence he could want to put something in, and he puts nothing in it.
In the corner the woodstove ticks.

choices.text: “It was a big month for Facebook.”
choices.key: At Hale’s, Lena asked why she had to find out about your girlfriend from a Facebook status. You made a joke. It died.
response: It dies in the air over the sheet cake. Caleb, who would laugh at anything tonight, doesn’t.
She doesn’t dignify it. She doesn’t even look up.

choices.key: At Hale’s, Lena asked why she had to find out about your girlfriend from a Facebook status. You started to say you didn’t know how, and stopped.
response: He stops. The end of the sentence is the thing he can’t say, and he hears the place in the air where it would go.
She waits exactly as long as it takes to be sure it isn’t coming.

s13c.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:33 PM · HALE’S, THE DOOR ON TRESTLES
body: It’s Hale who moves, and he does it gently, which is the only rescue he’s got. “Sarah, Miss Broussard?”
“Sarah,” Lena says, and sits down.

She finishes on the book, at an ordinary volume, to Hale. “Sarah wasn’t cruel because she left him. People leave. She was cruel because she let him believe he’d been replaced. Two years. He paid a man to follow her around London and read the reports at night, which houses she went into, how long she stayed, and he hated some man he’d never met. Henry thought it was a man too. Parkis thought so. Everybody did. She let every one of them believe the cheapest thing there was, because the true thing was harder to say.” She closes the Greene. “She let him think it was a man.”
In the corner the woodstove ticks.
*Replaced.* Jack hears it, and thinks of a week.

body.text: She looks at him once, at the end, down the whole length of the door, and it isn’t a win, on her face or on his.
Hale reaches for the bottle instead of a pen. At the far end Lena lays her pencil across the closed Greene. The point is hers, and she doesn’t look up from it.

body: Hale doesn’t try to start it again.

She’s up first. She takes her coat off the back of the chair, and Laney is up with her, leaving the Pyrex where it is with half the cake still in it, and the two of them come the length of the room on the far side of the door from him. At the screen door Lena finds her phone in Berkeley’s bowl without having to look and goes out onto the step.
Laney stops in the doorway beside Theo’s chair with the pink BlackBerry in her hand and says it low, down to him, where Jack can hear it perfectly well.
“Sugar, that was not about a *book*.”
“No,” says Theo.
The screen door slaps behind her. Theo is still holding the Rioja by the neck, with the price sticker turned into his palm.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. I told her what Danny asked about the third. If Pop won’t get out of the truck, she says, I get in. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. She asked if I asked Ma who the candle was for. No. You don’t. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks. I know what that means. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it. New Year’s Day I called her from the garage at the half, and she said, You called *me*. Saturday night she called the house — Ma answered and talked to her for ten minutes. Two hours on the kitchen phone, her mother’s cordless dying twice. Her grandmother made the christening gown for Luc in 1985; it rode out the storm in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. She had me be the priest so she could practice the promises. She thinks Binx doesn’t stop looking — he stops looking by himself. I told her Danny asked me something I can’t answer yet; she didn’t ask what. She asked how California was. ‘Come back, Youngstown.’ Two hours, and she never said Julian’s name. Lucille was baptized in the third quarter, and she didn’t get one word wrong. After that I called every night. Twelfth Night she got the baby in the king cake. Friday she said she hasn’t been fair to Julian, and she’s going to fix it. Sunday she landed: come find me tomorrow. Monday I couldn’t find her — not at 217, not at the twelve-ten. She came into Hale’s seminar a step behind him with a king cake, and the only chair left was next to mine. She was polite to me for fifteen minutes. Then Dido. Tuesday morning Julian put up a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late. She’s tagged. She’d said call me after. I didn’t. At the mailboxes she asked about my break, and I told her as far as Denver, and Ma’s words about the coffee. ‘Tell her I’m glad.’ The baptism was lovely. Tuesday night at St. Brendan’s she had the whole thing organized by half past eight, in a whisper, and put me on the table with Becca. When the TV said trapped she left the room. Julian went. Wednesday at the table she met Skye. She said no pictures at the table, and I argued with her about it in front of everybody. That night at the desk: Skye’s envelope was the biggest. ‘Tell her thank you. From Newman.’ Thursday she took the far end of Hale’s table before anybody got there. She moved the Saints to Sully’s. Saturday in the back hall she said she changed her mind, and stood up for Laney, and said Skye gave a good performance, and wouldn’t say what she meant. At Atlanta she kept my chair till the half. At ten after three she told me the time. Wednesday at three in the morning, the aftershock, in the Fishbowl: she said I could stop whatever I’m doing. I don’t know what I’m doing. Thursday Hale read her whole name off his list. She told him Lena. Saturday she ran the van to San Francisco. Six hours, row three. She asked me if I was happy. I said yes. At the end of the Walk I asked her how she had the nerve to be mad at me. She didn’t answer. She thanked me for coming and left. Monday, when Caleb said I was on a blog, she turned a page. Hale gave her Sarah Miles to prosecute and me Sarah to defend. Wednesday at his house, with the President on, she didn’t touch her wine. A website on Monday, a bed on Tuesday, an iPad before lunch — she had the whole week. She said she had to find out about my girlfriend from a Facebook status, when we talked every single day for weeks. I didn’t have an answer. Sarah let him think it was a man, she said. She walked home up Del Playa with Laney.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’ MLK Day he shoveled sand one-handed for Sigma Rho with Hollis in the other. At midnight Wednesday he pitched me a movie about a man whose friend got dumped and was with somebody else in a week. He said it twice. Hollis made his week. Theo’s in. He’s keeping the egg. Saturday he became a brother. Sunday he runs. He was correct to Lena for seven hours at Sully’s and sent me the end of it. He started on Julian, and I told him to stop. Monday he asked me, hypothetically, where a man who doesn’t go to Sully’s watches the Super Bowl. Made himself my plus-one to Hale’s, with a bottle that had a story. At Hale’s door Laney told him that wasn’t about a book. He said no.

s14.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:37 PM · HALE’S DECK — THE BLUFF
body: He goes out through the slider onto the deck, because it’s the only door in the house that doesn’t lead past anybody. The fog hasn’t come in. The moon is high and white, nearly full, and at the foot of the bluff the surf is loud in the dark. The bench at the rail is wet. The last time he was out here she was on it, with the dog’s head in her lap. He doesn’t sit on it.

The deck turns the corner of the house, and from the corner he can see a long way up Del Playa under the streetlights. Two of them are walking up the middle of the lane, Laney’s arm through Lena’s. Halfway up, a garage on the ocean side has its door rolled up and its light on, and a guitar case leaning in the doorway; they walk past it and don’t go in. Jack watches them until the lane bends and there is only the lane.

Somewhere at the back of his head a song starts up, one he knows the name of, and he stops it at the first line. The ends of his fingers are going on the rail, the way they went at the curb on Saturday.
Out past the end of the cliff, across the black water, the old Point Marisol Light stands where it stands, dark.

The slider rolls behind him. Hale comes out with a glass in one hand and the RAZR in the other, and puts the RAZR in Jack’s hand. “The only one in the bowl that folds,” he says. Jack puts it in his pocket without opening it. Hale goes to the rail a few feet down and stands there looking at the water, not at Jack, and doesn’t mention the last half hour. After a minute he holds the glass out sideways. Jack shakes his head, and Hale drinks it himself.
“I have to be somewhere at eight,” Jack says.
“Where,” says Hale, “does a Catholic go at eight o’clock on a Wednesday?”
“Where do you think?”
Hale looks out at the moon over the water. “Give him my regards,” he says. “He blessed my dog.” He takes his glass back inside.

It finds Jack at the rail as soon as he’s alone: first at the back of his mouth, then in his hands. The pack is in the inside pocket of the Carhartt with the lighter. The tin is in the other pocket, where it has ridden since Christmas.

body.text: The last one was after midnight on Saturday, on the low wall under the olive tree at St. Brendan’s, with the van’s engine cooling.
The last one was a week ago tonight, in the roof door at Delgado, with the rain coming in on his knees.

body: Through the glass behind him Evan is stacking jam jars in Hale’s sink.

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it. I owe him more than one. Gave me a pocket Housman for Danny, foxed, wartime. No margins. They’d only erase them. Has a deaf old greyhound named Bishop Berkeley. Brought him to the Blessing of the Animals to annoy Fr. Osei. Osei finished his limerick for him. Asked me if the Housman had gone. Says when you leave something, look at it. Newman did. Threw a dinner at the cliff end of Del Playa. Told a man asking Yusuf about Fort Hood that Yusuf’s a guest, not a spokesman. Read our margins out loud. Stopped in the middle of Lena’s, and folded it away. Told Caleb he doesn’t answer devotion. Collected our margins. Read Lena’s on mine: Neither do I. The final’s oral, December 16th — each of us defends the other’s best argument, and he’s the opponent. Told the room to keep Yusuf’s chair. The last seminar: Lena said nothing for an hour, and he told us to note the date. By Friday we each email him which of the other’s arguments we’ll defend. If we pick a weak one, he’ll know. Both picks came in. Not surprised, not disappointed — at his age the same thing as joy. Wednesday, two o’clock. Come as you are. The oral: she’d sent him Augustine. Lena first, then me. He knew which one I’d picked. I don’t yet know what I know, he said. He said it was an argument; he’s told they still occur. Marks posted on the solstice. I did well, which he’d like me to understand is not the same as being right. He and Berkeley are spending Christmas in Marisol. Spring: PHIL 109H, The Novel as Moral Argument, Mondays and Thursdays at one in Hollis 302. Opposite ends of the table, for the safety of the others. He got the baby in the king cake. ‘For the first quarter of an hour you were civil, and I didn’t care for it. I find I care for this even less.’ Carthage is not on the syllabus. The Conversion of St. Paul: he did Saul for Caleb. He’s in New York Thursday, being rude to a churchman on a stage, so Greene moved to his house Wednesday with the State of the Union on — phones in the dog’s bowl, bring a guest, sides assigned: me for Sarah’s silence, Lena against. Opposite ends of a door. He turned the President off before the rebuttal. On the deck he asked where a Catholic goes at eight on a Wednesday. Give him my regards. He blessed my dog.

choices.key: On Hale’s deck, after the fight, you lit one.
response: He lights it with his back to Hale’s window, cupping the lighter against the wind off the water. The first pull is everything he wanted out of it; the rest is only smoke, and he smokes it anyway, down to the filter, watching the surf come white out of the dark.
He puts it out on the wet rail and pockets the end, and at five to eight he goes down the deck stairs to the lane, late, smelling of it, on his way to confession.

choices.key: On Hale’s deck, after the fight, you put the pack back.
response: He takes his hand out of the jacket empty and puts both hands on the rail, where the salt has left it wet, and leaves them there until his fingers have forgotten what they were after.
At five to eight he goes down the deck stairs to the lane, fast and late, with nothing lit.

choices.key: On Hale’s deck, after the fight, you counted her eleven.
response: He takes the tin out and opens it on the rail in the light from Hale’s window. RELIQUARY on the lid, in her hand.

Eleven. Eleven under the olive tree on Saturday night. Eleven now. He closes it, and puts it back where it rides, and at five to eight goes down the deck stairs to the lane, late, with the weight of it against his side on every step.

choices.key: On Hale’s deck, after the fight, you counted her eleven.
response: He takes the tin out instead and opens it on the rail, in the light from Hale’s window, for the first time this year. RELIQUARY, in her hand, on the lid.

He counts them with a fingertip and gets eleven, and counts again in case, and gets eleven. Same as December. He shuts it and puts it away, and at five to eight goes down the deck stairs to the lane, late.
